title: Australia's 'Mushroom Murderer' Erin Patterson Begins Appeal Against Life Sentence
excerpt: Victoria's Court of Appeal will hear arguments from both Patterson's defense and prosecutors, who say her 33-year sentence is too lenient.
body:
• Erin Patterson, 51, convicted of murdering three in-laws with death cap mushrooms in a beef Wellington, begins her appeal at Victoria's Court of Appeal on August 19
  • Patterson is challenging the conviction on grounds of improperly admitted evidence, unfair cross-examination, and jury irregularity involving a shared hotel with media
  • Prosecutors are simultaneously appealing her 33-year non-parole period as "manifestly inadequate"

An Australian court will on Wednesday begin hearing the appeal of Erin Patterson, the woman convicted of murdering three of her estranged husband's relatives by feeding them a beef Wellington laced with deadly death cap mushrooms — a case that captivated audiences worldwide and spawned multiple podcasts and books.

Patterson, 51, was convicted last year of murdering three elderly in-laws and sentenced to life in prison with a non-parole period of 33 years, one of the longest sentences ever given to a woman in Australia. She has maintained her innocence throughout, insisting the deaths were accidental.

The Case That Gripped a Nation

A 12-person jury found that Patterson lured her mother-in-law Gail Patterson, father-in-law Donald Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson to a lunch at her home in Leongatha, a town of about 6,000 people roughly 135 kilometers southeast of Melbourne, in 2023. She served them beef Wellingtons containing toxic death cap mushrooms — the world's most lethal fungus.

https://x.com/7NewsBrisbane/status/2089572053644906840

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, Heather's husband, who survived the poisoned meal. Her estranged husband Simon had been invited but pulled out on the eve of the lunch, texting Patterson that he felt "uncomfortable" attending. At the time, the couple — still legally married — were fighting over child support contributions, according to AFP.

The 11-week trial in the nearby country town of Morwell drew intense global interest, with major outlets including Bloomberg, the BBC, and The Guardian providing extensive coverage.

Grounds for Appeal

Patterson is appealing on several grounds, according to court documents. Her legal team alleges a "substantial miscarriage of justice" occurred during the trial. Specifically, her lawyers argue that a "fundamental irregularity" took place while the jury was sequestered — an error that led to jurors being housed at the same hotel as some members of the media, which they say "fatally undermined the integrity of the verdicts."

"Various pieces of evidence introduced, including cell tower location data and messages from Facebook friends, were either irrelevant or unfairly prejudicial."

— Patterson's appeal filing

Patterson's lawyer also accused the prosecution of conducting an "unfair and oppressive" cross-examination. Additionally, the defense argues that some evidence submitted and accepted by the judge was not relevant, while other evidence that should have been admitted was excluded.

Patterson's legal team enlisted Julian McMahon, a prominent human rights barrister, to handle the appeal. The conviction appeal and sentence appeal have been listed for hearing on August 19 and 20.

Prosecutors Push for Harsher Sentence

In an unusual twist, Victoria's Court of Appeal will simultaneously hear a separate appeal from prosecutors, who filed their challenge in October describing Patterson's sentence as "manifestly inadequate." If successful, the prosecution's appeal could result in an even longer non-parole period for Patterson.

During sentencing, Patterson's legal team had argued she should be eligible for parole after 30 years rather than 33, citing the notoriety of her case, which they said would likely mean she would spend most of her prison sentence in isolation.

What's Next

The appeal hearings are scheduled for two days at the Court of Appeal in Melbourne. A decision is not expected immediately — appeals of this nature typically take weeks or months for judges to deliver their findings. The outcome could range from the conviction being upheld or overturned to a retrial being ordered, or Patterson's sentence being increased if prosecutors prevail on their cross-appeal.

The case has inspired several true crime podcasts and at least one book, and continues to generate significant public interest in Australia and internationally.
